name: brainFOOD
title: Eight commands and a row of boxes
intro: Picture a long row of boxes, each holding a number that starts at 0, and a pointer that sits under one box. brainFOOD has just eight commands to move the pointer, change the number in a box, read and print characters, and loop. That is enough to compute anything a bigger language can, just very slowly and with a lot of plus signs. Every other character is ignored, so you can write notes anywhere.

lessons.title: The eight commands
lessons.summary: Move, change, print, read and loop.

sections.p: > move right to the next box · < move left · + add 1 to this box · - take 1 away · . print this box as a character · , read a typed character into this box · [ if this box is 0, skip past the matching ] · ] if this box is not 0, go back to the matching [.
. prints the character whose code is in the box: 65 is A, 97 is a, 48 is 0, 10 is a new line. So to print a letter you first count up to its code.
Seventy-two plus signs is a lot. A loop does it faster: put 8 in box 0, and each time round add 9 to box 1 and take 1 from box 0. When box 0 reaches 0 the loop stops and box 1 holds 8 × 9 = 72.

practice.why: 8 × 8 = 64, plus one is 65, the code for A.
It keeps taking 1 away until the box is 0, then the loop ends.
6 × 8 = 48 is the character 0; each +. adds one and prints again.

practice.q: How many boxes does the pointer move in >>><?
practice.why: Three steps right, one step left.

practice.q: What happens to a letter like x in a program?
practice.why: Only the eight command symbols mean anything.
5 × 13 = 65, the code for A.
7 × 7 = 49, the code for the character 1.

options: Reads one typed character into the current box
practice.answer: Reads one typed character into the current box
practice.why: Comma is input; the box gets the character's code.

lessons.title: Hello World, step by step
lessons.summary: Setting up several boxes with one loop.

sections.p: A classic trick: one loop fills several boxes at once with handy starting values, and then small nudges reach each letter. Here box 0 counts down from 10 while boxes 1 to 4 grow by 7, 10, 3 and 1, giving 70, 100, 30 and 10. Those are close to H (72), the lowercase letters (around 100), a space (32) and a new line (10).
, stores the code of one typed character. This program echoes each character until it reads a 0 (end of input on most interpreters).

practice.why: Box 0 counts the 10 rounds down to 0; box 1 gains 7 each round.
5 × 13 = 65 is A; three more is 68, D.

practice.q: Why is the program text full of words like H and space?
options: They are notes; non-commands are ignored
practice.answer: They are notes; non-commands are ignored
practice.why: Any character that is not one of the eight commands is skipped.
5 × 13 = 65 is A; four more is 69, E.
65 + 1 is B; each +. prints the next letter.

options: Echoes each typed character until it reads a 0
practice.answer: Echoes each typed character until it reads a 0
practice.why: It reads, then loops printing and reading until a 0 ends the loop.

lessons.title: Moving and copying
lessons.summary: Clearing a box, moving a value and copying it with a helper box.

sections.p: Most brainFOOD programs are built from a few small patterns. The first: [-] sets a box to 0, whatever it held. The second moves a value: [->+<] takes 1 from this box and adds 1 to the next, over and over, until this box is empty.
sections.code:
++++++++[>++++++++<-]>+    box 1 is 65
[->>+<<]                   move it two boxes along
>>.                        box 3 prints A

sections.p: Moving one value onto another adds them. Box 0 holds 3, box 1 holds 4; moving box 0 into box 1 leaves 7 there. Adding 48 then turns the number 7 into the character 7.
sections.code:
+++>++++<     box 0 is 3 and box 1 is 4
[->+<]        move box 0 into box 1
>             box 1 is 7
>++++++[<++++++++>-]<     add 6 times 8 to box 1
.

sections.p: Moving empties the box you move from. To copy, move into two boxes at once, then move one of them back. Afterwards box 0 still holds 5 and box 1 holds a copy.
sections.code:
+++++          box 0 is 5
[->+>+<<]      box 1 and box 2 both get 5 and box 0 is empty
>>[-<<+>>]     move box 2 back into box 0
++++++[<++++++++<++++++++>>-]     add 48 to boxes 0 and 1
<<.>.

sections.p: Inside a loop, count your arrows. If the body moves right two and left two, the pointer is back on the counting box when ] checks it. If they do not balance, the loop tests a different box each round, which is almost always a bug.

practice.q: What does [-] do to the current box?
practice.why: It keeps taking 1 away until the box is 0, then the loop ends.
Box 1 gets 66 (8 × 8 + 2), which is then moved to box 2 and printed: B.
Moving empties box 0 into box 1.

practice.q: Why does copying use a third box?
options: Moving empties the source, so one copy has to be moved back
Boxes can only hold one value
practice.answer: Moving empties the source, so one copy has to be moved back
practice.why: The value goes into two boxes, then one of them refills the original.
2 moved onto 3 gives 5; then 48 is built two boxes along and moved on top, giving the character 5.
3 is moved into box 1, then 48 is added so it prints as the character 3.
65 is built in box 1, moved two boxes along, and printed from box 3.
Moving empties the source box into the next one.

lessons.title: Subtracting and multiplying
lessons.summary: Taking one box from another, and loops inside loops.

sections.p: Subtracting is moving with a minus: [->-<] takes 1 from both boxes until the first is empty. Here box 0 holds 7 and box 1 holds 3; taking box 1 away from box 0 leaves 4.
sections.code:
+++++++>+++    box 0 is 7 and box 1 is 3
[-<->]<        take box 1 away from box 0
>++++++[<++++++++>-]<     add 48
.

sections.p: To multiply box 0 by box 1, add box 1 into box 2 once for every unit in box 0. Each round copies box 1 (using box 3 as the helper) so it survives for the next round. That is a loop inside a loop.
sections.code:
++>++++<       box 0 is 2 and box 1 is 4
[
  >[->+>+<<]   add box 1 to box 2 and box 3
  >>[-<<+>>]   move box 3 back to box 1
  <<<-         one round done
]
>>>++++++[<++++++++>-]<.  box 2 is 8

sections.p: Each box holds 0 to 255. Taking 1 from 0 gives 255, and adding 1 to 255 gives 0. Some interpreters do not wrap, so careful programs avoid relying on it.

practice.why: 9 take away 4 is 5, plus 48 is the character 5.

practice.q: In the multiply program, why is box 1 copied each round?
options: Adding it to box 2 would otherwise empty it
practice.answer: Adding it to box 2 would otherwise empty it
practice.why: Moving empties the source; copying keeps box 1 ready for the next round.
The first loop makes 3 × 3 = 9 in box 1; then 48 is built and added to it.

practice.q: With wrapping, what is in a box after 0 then -?
practice.why: Boxes hold 0 to 255 and wrap around at both ends.
8 take away 3 is 5, plus 48 is the character 5.
2 × 4 is built in box 2 by the nested loops; then 48 turns it into the character 8.
3 × 2 = 6 in box 1; adding 48 prints the digit 6.

lessons.title: Counting loops
lessons.summary: A counter box, a working box, and loops inside loops.

sections.p: A counting loop keeps the count in one box and does its work in another. Here box 0 counts 5 rounds and box 1 starts at A, printing and growing by one each round.
sections.code:
+++++                       box 0 counts 5
>++++++++[>++++++++<-]>+    box 2 is 65 which is A
<<[>>.+<<-]                 print and step five times

sections.p: The same shape works backwards. Box 0 counts 10 rounds and box 2 starts at the character 9 (57).
Put one counting loop inside another to draw a grid. Box 0 counts rows, box 1 holds a star (42), box 2 a new line (10), and box 3 counts the stars on each row.

practice.why: The loop prints box 2 three times but never changes it.
Box 2 starts at 68 (D) and grows by one each of the four rounds.

practice.q: Why does the grid program use box 3 for the stars on each row?
options: Box 3 is refilled every row, while box 0 keeps the row count
practice.answer: Box 3 is refilled every row, while box 0 keeps the row count
practice.why: Each loop needs its own counter, or the inner loop would use up the outer one.

practice.q: A loop body moves right three times and left twice. What goes wrong?
options: The loop checks a different box each round
practice.answer: The loop checks a different box each round
practice.why: The pointer drifts one box right per round, so ] no longer tests the counter.
Box 2 starts at A and grows by one across three counted rounds.
Box 2 holds a star (42) and the outer count prints it four times.
Five rounds print the same box without changing it.

lessons.title: Decisions
lessons.summary: Doing something only if a box is not zero, and if/else with a flag.

sections.p: brainFOOD has no if, but a loop that empties its own box runs at most once. [ do something [-] ] means “if this box is not 0, do something”. Here box 0 holds 1, so the letter is printed; with 0 it would be skipped.
sections.code:
+                            box 0 is 1
>++++++++[>+++++++++++<-]>+  box 2 is 89 which is Y
<<[>>.<<[-]]                 if box 0 then print

sections.p: For an else, keep a flag box set to 1. The “then” part clears the flag; afterwards, a second one-time loop on the flag runs only if the “then” part did not. This program subtracts box 1 from box 0 and says Y if they were equal, N if not. Box 3 holds N and box 4 holds Y.
sections.code:
>>++++++++[>++++++++++>+++++++++++<<-]>-->+<<<<
+++++>+++++    box 0 and box 1 are both 5
[-<->]<        box 0 is the difference
>+<            box 1 is the flag
[>>>.<<<[-]>-<]    not zero so print N and clear the flag
>[>>>.<<<-]<       flag still set so print Y

sections.h: Both paths end in the same place
sections.p: Each one-time loop must finish on the box it started from, with that box at 0. Otherwise the program carries on from a different box depending on which way it went, and the rest of the program breaks.

practice.why: Box 0 is 0, so the one-time loop is skipped entirely.
5 take away 3 is 2, not zero, so N is printed and the flag is cleared.

practice.q: Why does an if-loop end with [-]?
options: So the loop runs at most once
practice.answer: So the loop runs at most once
practice.why: Emptying its own box makes the ] check fail, so the loop exits.

practice.q: What is the flag box for?
options: Remembering whether the then part ran, so the else part can be skipped
practice.answer: Remembering whether the then part ran, so the else part can be skipped
practice.why: The then part clears the flag; the else part runs only if it is still set.
Box 0 holds 2, so the one-time loop still runs once: it prints A and then clears itself.
The flag box is 1, so the if-loop prints A and empties itself.

lessons.title: Words in memory
lessons.summary: Storing letters in a row of boxes and walking along them.

sections.p: A word can live in a row of boxes with a 0 at each end. [.>] prints boxes and moves right until it reaches a 0; [<] or [.<] goes back the other way. Here one loop builds o, a and k (111, 97, 107) together.
sections.code:
++++++++++[>+++++++++++>++++++++++>+++++++++++<<<-]
>+>--->---     boxes 1 to 3 hold o a k
<<[.>]         print forwards until box 4
<[.<]          print backwards until box 0

sections.p: Walking a word lets you change each letter. Lowercase letters are 32 above their capitals, so taking 32 from each box shouts the word. The loop stops at the 0 after the last letter.

options: When the pointer reaches a box holding 0
practice.answer: When the pointer reaches a box holding 0
practice.why: The loop test checks the current box; a 0 ends the walk.
Boxes 1 and 2 become 65 and 66, and the walk prints both before stopping at box 3.

practice.q: Why keep a 0 box before the start of a word?
options: So a backwards walk like [<] knows where to stop
So the word prints in capitals
practice.answer: So a backwards walk like [<] knows where to stop
practice.why: Walks stop at 0, so zeros at both ends mark the edges of the word.
Boxes 1–3 hold 65–67; [.>] walks right printing until the trailing 0.
A forward walk prints AB, then a backward walk prints BA.
Forwards to the end prints ABC; backwards prints CBA.

lessons.title: Putting it together: the alphabet
lessons.summary: Building numbers with loops and printing a whole sequence.

sections.p: To print the alphabet, a counter of 26 and a letter that starts at A are enough. Building 26 as 5 × 5 + 1 and 65 as 8 × 8 + 1 keeps the program short.

Everything bigger in brainFOOD is built from the patterns in this course: clear, move, copy, count, if and walk. Good next challenges: print the alphabet backwards, print the lowercase alphabet with a new line every 13 letters, or read characters with , and print them in capitals. An online visualiser that shows the row of boxes as the program runs makes debugging much easier.

practice.why: Box 1 starts at 90 (Z) and the loop prints it, then takes 1 away, five times.

practice.q: Which is the shortest way to put 64 in a box?
practice.why: ++++++++[>++++++++<-] is 19 commands instead of 64.

practice.q: Which pattern prints every box until a 0?
practice.why: Print, move right, and repeat while the box is not 0.
Three counted rounds print A, then B, then C.
Box 2 starts at 67 (C) and steps up across four rounds.
Box 2 starts at Z and counts down three times.

lessons.title: Comparing two boxes
lessons.summary: Subtract to test equality, then choose Y or N with a flag.

sections.p: To ask whether two boxes hold the same number, subtract one from the other until the second is empty: [-<->]< leaves the difference in the first box. Zero means equal. Combine that with the flag pattern from the decisions lesson: print Y when the difference is 0, N otherwise.
Same scaffolding, but box 1 starts at 3 instead of 5. The difference is not zero, so N prints and the flag is cleared.

Both branches must finish on the same box with the tested cells cleared. If the “equal” path leaves the pointer two cells further right than the “not equal” path, every later command is aimed at the wrong box.

practice.why: 5 − 5 = 0, so the flag path prints Y.
5 − 3 ≠ 0, so N prints and the flag clears.

practice.q: What does [-<->]< leave in the first box?
options: The difference of the two boxes
practice.answer: The difference of the two boxes
practice.why: Each round takes one from both until the second is empty.

practice.q: Why clear the flag in the “not equal” branch?
options: So the equal/Y branch does not also run
The loop needs a non-zero flag
practice.answer: So the equal/Y branch does not also run
practice.why: The Y loop runs only while the flag is still set.
3 and 3 are equal.

practice.q: What must both branches agree on before the program continues?
options: Pointer position and which boxes are zero
The value of every box in memory
practice.answer: Pointer position and which boxes are zero
practice.why: Otherwise later code depends on which way you branched.

lessons.title: Capitals and small letters
lessons.summary: Adding or taking 32, and walking a word to shout it.

sections.p: In ASCII, a lowercase letter is 32 above its capital. Adding 32 turns A (65) into a (97). A short loop of four rounds adding eight builds that 32, then a move adds it onto the letter.
Store a lowercase word with zeros at the ends, take 32 from each letter, then walk and print. Here oak becomes OAK.
Digit characters sit at 48–57. They are not 32 away from letters, so the ±32 trick is only for A–Z. To show a numeric value as a digit character, add 48 (six rounds of eight) as in earlier lessons.

practice.why: Each letter loses 32, then a forward walk prints them.

practice.q: How far apart are A and a in ASCII?
Why does the shout program take 32 from every box before printing?
options: To turn lowercase codes into capitals
practice.answer: To turn lowercase codes into capitals
practice.why: Minus 32 maps a→A, b→B, and so on.

practice.q: What number do you add to turn a count like 7 into the character 7?
practice.why: Digit characters start at code 48 for 0.
64 in the box plus 6 is 70, the code for F.

lessons.title: Project: HI then a newline
lessons.summary: Two letters and a line break from one short tape.

sections.p: Build H and i the usual way, print them, then set a box to 10 and print the newline. A tiny complete program that moves, loops and prints.

practice.q: What character code is a newline?
practice.why: ASCII line feed is 10.
